# Write in Markdown, get a live document

`qmd-fast` renders `.qmd` to HTML with **instant, block-level updates** — save the
file and only the block you changed re-renders, in place, with scroll and live
state preserved.

It speaks the things technical writing actually needs, all rendered offline:

- **Math**, server-side via KaTeX: inline $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$ and display —
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}\,dx = \sqrt{\pi}$$
- **Diagrams**, from fenced code:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  write["write .qmd"] --> preview["live preview"]
  preview --> edit["edit a block"]
  edit -->|"only that block"| preview
  preview --> publish["build → static HTML"]
```

- **Callouts**, for the asides that documentation lives on:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Block-level updates
Every top-level element is a block with a content-hash id. A save diffs the new
blocks against the old and ships only the differences over a websocket.
:::

# Why it feels fast

There is no per-edit startup cost. The server stays warm and so does the Jupyter
kernel, so editing a cell re-runs just that cell and everything downstream — not
the whole document.

::: {.callout-note}
## Click to source
Double-click any block in the preview and your editor jumps to the exact line it
came from, even across `{{< include >}}`d files.
:::

A second screenful of prose so the demo has somewhere to scroll: the block model
is the one idea everything keys off — source mapping, incremental re-render, and
live-state preservation all build on it. Code-cell outputs are themselves blocks,
keyed to their cell, so a re-run swaps the figure in place without touching the
rest of the page.
